segments.text: This is the cockpit of a brand new type of airplane, and almost everything you'd use to fly a normal plane is missing.
The yoke, the rubber pedals, even the trim wheel isn't here.
It's like sitting in a car that has no steering wheel to guide it.
And here's the craziest part.
To fly this plane, there's only one small stick.
That's it.
This plane is called the Skytron, and it was designed to eliminate all human pilot error.
It turns out around 80% of small plane crashes come down to pilot error, not broken parts.
And it's not because the pilots are bad, it's just that flying a plane requires the pilot to do so many things at once.
So Skytron's building a plane that helps prevent pilot mistakes.
If you pull the stick all the way back, the plane won't stall or fall out of the sky.
And if you point it at a mountain, it won't go.
And if you try to spin it erratically, it won't either.
There are three flight computers that vote on every action.
And if two outvote the one, it won't make the maneuver.
You also have two engines in this plane, so if one quits, the other can fly you home.
And of course, if everything fails, there's a parachute that pops that will safely lower the plane to the ground.
The goal of the Skytron plane is to make flying 99% autonomous.
You type in where you're going, it takes off, talks to air traffic control, and it lands.
The guy behind this project's name is Greg Mercer.
And he got into this because he sold a software company, started to learn to fly, and he hated how old planes felt.
So he's putting $20 million of his own money to try to reinvent small plane aviation.
Now, right now, Skytron is a wooden mock-up, but the first demo flight is scheduled for later this year.
And if it works, Greg might be spearheading a whole new category of aviation.
